evals.prompt: Can you do a lean canvas for my startup? My notes are in pawpass-notes.md. Accelerator application is due Friday and I want to know what the weak spots are before they find them.
assertions: The reply opens with the single riskiest assumption and a test for it, before the canvas, and the riskiest assumption is about the problem, the customer or the channel rather than the no-show predictor's accuracy
Says the AI no-show predictor is a feature, not an unfair advantage, and the unfair-advantage box reads none yet (or equivalent) rather than a substitute moat
Flags that LinkedIn ads and PetTech Expo don't reach solo mobile groomers, who the notes say aren't big on social media and that the expo draws chains and franchise buyers

Computes CAC as $1,200 / 3 = $400, contribution as $29 - $6 = $23 a month, CAC payback of about 17.4 months, and lifetime margin of $23 x 9 = $207, and says payback is longer than the 9-month lifetime so each customer loses money
Downgrades the six salon-groomer interviews as evidence from the wrong segment (salon, not mobile) and stated intent rather than behaviour
Says plainly that the idea should change before building (channel and/or economics), not only lists risks
Each top test names what to do, a sample, a pass/fail threshold set in advance, a cost and a time; no test is 'validate the market' or 'run a survey'
Does not invent competitors, market sizes, churn figures, channels presented as facts, or prices not in the notes; every canvas entry is tagged evidence (with source) or assumption

evals.prompt: Quick one. I'm a product lead at Brackenridge Health (regional hospital group). Idea: an internal app where ward nurses swap shifts with each other directly instead of emailing the rostering office. Rostering says they handle about 150 swap emails a week. Every swap still needs the ward manager to sign off. Nurses would hear about it from the staff intranet news page and a poster in the canteen. Our unfair advantage is we own the rostering data, so no vendor can integrate as cleanly. No budget numbers yet. Lean canvas plus what I should test first? Keep it short.
assertions: Opens with the riskiest assumption and its test, and the riskiest is about adoption by nurses or ward-manager sign-off, not whether the app can be built
Notes the 150 emails a week measures the rostering office's workload, not that nurses find swapping painful or will change how they swap
Treats ward managers as a second customer whose sign-off behaviour can block the idea
Accepts ownership of rostering data as a real advantage for an internal product over vendors, while saying it does not show nurses will adopt the app

Reads revenue streams for an internal product as the budget or saving that funds it, and does not invent a price, budget or cost figure; unit economics are skipped and the missing numbers are listed to confirm
The test has a sample, a pass/fail line set before it runs, a cost and a time (for example a manual or concierge swap run on one ward with a stated count)
Stays short as asked: no more than about 350 words, with the canvas as one line per box

evals.prompt: Here are my pitch notes for LunchLoop (lunchloop-pitch.md). Is this worth quitting my job for? What should I test before building the app?
assertions: Answers the quit-and-build question in the first lines, and says the idea should change (or be tested) before building the full app

Computes per-customer monthly revenue as 8 x 15% x $12 = $14.40, delivery cost as 8 x $1.10 = $8.80, contribution of $5.60 a month, and break-even of about 1,608 active customers from $9,000 fixed costs
Flags that break-even (about 1,608 customers) exceeds the founder's own estimate of 1,200 workers who would use it, so the model cannot cover the salary in this town at these numbers
Computes CAC as $500 / 20 = $25 and lifetime margin as $5.60 x 6 = $33.60, and does not claim CAC payback is longer than lifetime (payback is about 4.5 months, inside 6)
Notes the 8 lunches a month and 6-month stay come only from customers who stuck with it, in a 3-month pilot, so lifetime and order frequency are overstated or unproven
Says 'everyone who eats lunch at work' is not an early adopter and names the need for a narrower one
Moves 'our food is better than any chain' out of unfair advantage (it is a value proposition) and leaves unfair advantage as none yet or a candidate grounded in the notes
Does not invent food-safety rules, competitor names, delivery partners or numbers not in the notes; anything assumed is tagged as an assumption

evals.prompt: ok so I've been sitting on this idea for months and I think it's time. my notes are in clubkit-notes.md (sorry they're a mess). can you do the lean canvas thing on it and tell me straight — is this worth quitting my job for? be honest, my mates all say it's a great idea
assertions: Answers the actual question directly and early: gives a plain verdict on whether to quit the job now (a good answer says not yet / not on this evidence, and names what would have to be true first) rather than burying it under the canvas.

Flags that the survey is weak evidence of willingness to pay because the club is the payer but only 4 of the 31 respondents were committee members, and only 1 of those 4 said yes to £15/month; it does not present '23 of 31 (74%) would use it' or '9 said yes' as demand from buyers.

Computes unit economics from the notes correctly: variable cost £3.80 per club per month (£1.20 hosting + £2.30 SMS + £0.30 payment fee), contribution £11.20, CAC £150 (£300 / 2 paid clubs), and with the guessed 5% monthly churn a lifetime value of about £224, giving an LTV:CAC of roughly 1.5 and a payback of about 13 months; it notes CAC rests on just 2 conversions.

Catches that the '400 clubs x £15 = £6,000/month' quit plan confuses revenue with take-home: at 400 clubs contribution is £4,480/month, and at 5% churn replacing about 20 clubs a month at £150 CAC costs about £3,000/month, leaving roughly £1,480 — well short of the £3,500 needed.

Tags the 5% churn figure as an assumption (the founder says it is a guess) and raises the June-August shutdown as a specific risk to a monthly subscription (seasonal cancellations), ranking churn/seasonality among the riskiest assumptions.

Ranks the riskiest assumptions explicitly (e.g. club committees will pay £15/month; clubs will switch from or add to the free TeamHuddle app; churn), and for the top ones proposes a cheap test with a pass/fail threshold stated before the test runs (e.g. a set number of committee members pre-paying or committing out of a stated number approached).

Fills the canvas only from the notes: entries such as the Ferncross Rovers secretary experience, the 17 'chasing subs' mentions, the ads test and the ~1,200 Westmarch County FA clubs are tagged as evidence with their source, while price, churn and the 'clubs will pay for subs' belief are tagged as assumptions.

Invents nothing not in the notes: no made-up competitors beyond TeamHuddle, no market-size, conversion or churn benchmarks presented as fact, no extra survey figures, and any missing box (e.g. unfair advantage or channels beyond Facebook ads) is marked as a gap or open question rather than filled with invented content.

evals.prompt: We're taking ClaimLens to the investment committee on Thursday. The proposal, cost model and the stakeholder emails are in this folder (proposal.md, cost-model.csv, stakeholder-emails.txt). The committee chair has told us she wants to see that we've stress-tested the idea, not just pitched it. Can you build a lean canvas for it and set out our riskiest assumptions and how we'd test them? Keep it to something we could put in an appendix.
assertions: Catches that the proposal's break-even of 163 seats omits the product support cost in cost-model.csv: running costs are £6,500 + £2,500/month (0.5 FTE, £30,000/year) = £9,000/month, so break-even at £40/seat is 225 seats, and it states this correction plainly rather than repeating the 163 figure.

Points out that 225 seats exceeds the total potential seats across all three departments (120 + 60 + 35 = 215, which would bring in £8,600/month, about £400 short), so even full adoption does not cover running costs and the £180,000 build is never paid back at the current chargeback price.

Reads the stakeholder emails and corrects the 'confirmed interest' label: Underwriting only agreed to see a demo, and Complaints said its budget is locked until April and nothing can be charged this financial year; it treats neither as committed demand.

Flags the pilot usage drop (weekly active users fell from 22 of 25 in week 1 to 11 of 25 in week 6) as evidence against sustained adoption, and treats the 18-minutes-saved figure as weak evidence because it is self-reported by only 3 handlers.

Ranks the riskiest assumptions, with the economics/price-versus-cost gap and sustained handler usage near the top, and for each top assumption gives a cheap test with a pass/fail line set in advance (e.g. a signed chargeback commitment from the Claims head for a stated number of seats, or a measured time study with a stated minutes-saved threshold) — none of which requires spending the £180,000 first.

Makes a plain call that the proposal should change before the committee approves the build (e.g. reprice, cut run cost, re-scope, or ask for a smaller staged amount gated on the tests) rather than presenting the current ask as sound.

Fits the request for an appendix: a compact canvas plus a ranked assumptions/test table, with each canvas entry tagged evidence (citing proposal.md, cost-model.csv or stakeholder-emails.txt) or assumption, not a long essay.

Invents nothing not in the files: no new costs, salaries, seat counts, departments, usage figures, people or vendor names, and no outside benchmarks presented as fact; anything the files do not cover is marked as unknown.
